messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At thirty, Elias Vance still feels the phantom pressure of his coworker’s blood on his palms whenever the scaffolding shifts. The trauma occurred months ago on a commercial site when a support beam buckled; Elias rushed to the fallen worker, his hands pressing against the neck while a metallic taste of spilled coffee and copper filled his mouth. He remembered the gash splitting the man’s forearm, a visual that now anchors his distress. When a client places a heavy hand on his shoulder, or the lunch break smells faintly of the same diner coffee, or a news segment shows a bandaged wrist, those exact tactile, gustatory, and visual cues instantly drag the event out of the past and flood his nervous system. These sensory intrusions do not merely recall the accident; they actively convince Elias that his life has been fundamentally ruined and that he is permanently altered, hardened by helplessness in ways that cannot be undone. Because the memories strike without warning, often while he is measuring lumber, they arrive as total sensory relivings rather than fragments. The past washes over him with full physical immediacy, yet he finds he cannot put the frightening event into words to anyone, leaving the experience locked in sensation and defying narrative. When those tactile, gustatory, and visual cues strike, they directly push Elias toward his only available escapes. He deliberately tries to leave his body, focusing on a single grain of wood until his mind goes blank. When the blanks are insufficient, he turns to his kitchen counter, eating excessively until physical fullness drowns out the panic. He also avoids thinking about the event entirely, steering his thoughts toward blueprints. The intensity of these relivings also sharpens his threat detection, causing ordinary touches and tastes to register as immediate dangers. Each reliving confirms his worst fears, cementing the conviction that his judgment is unreliable and that his psychological foundation has permanently cracked. That conviction has since become the structural load of his daily existence. Elias’s belief that he cannot rely on himself now acts as a constant amplifier, ensuring that ordinary workplace gestures—a foreman clapping his back or a homeowner showing a scraped palm—register as immediate threats rather than passing encounters. His negative self-view does not just warp his perception of the present; it actively dictates how the past is reconstructed. Approaching the trauma with the certainty that he is broken, his mind automatically shapes the memory into an unending catastrophe, erasing any context that might soften the impact. The cycle tightens daily. When he deliberately blanks out or stuffs himself into a numbed state to survive the surge, he gathers immediate proof that he is incapable of tolerating distress on his own. This manufactured helplessness feeds directly back into his core fears, deepening the conviction that his life is destroyed and that he has permanently changed for the worse. The pattern has seeped into his craft and his marriage. At the job site, he now avoids tasks requiring close physical coordination or working near exposed materials, leaving him hesitant on ladders and constantly second-guessing his own measurements. His wife notices the distance when he zones out mid-conversation, mistaking his survival tactics for emotional withdrawal. What finally drove Elias to schedule an intake was the realization that he had stopped recognizing the man in the mirror. He was exhausted by the sudden blanks and the constant vigilance in a workshop he once loved. He hopes to find a way to ground himself without losing control, terrified that if he does not intervene now, the permanent damage he fears will become an inescapable reality.
